targets.description: The article reports Michael Antoniou's argument that regulatory conclusions of glyphosate safety rest on inadequate and industry-shaped testing.
The opposing position includes regulatory reliance on glyphosate-only tests, industry-sponsored studies, accepted exposure limits, and the claim that the targeted plant pathway is absent in humans.
The rebuttal distinguishes pure glyphosate from more toxic commercial formulations while still alleging harms from glyphosate itself.
The article uses formulation, mixture, microbiome, low-dose animal, and carcinogenicity evidence to dispute the safety conclusion.
Regulators test isolated glyphosate rather than complete products encountered in practice
Industry-sponsored evidence and eligibility rules shape regulatory safety assessments
Single-pesticide testing does not represent real-world chemical mixtures
The plant-pathway safety argument overlooks effects on the human microbiome
Independent low-dose and lifetime animal findings are presented as inconsistent with current safety limits

targets.excerpt: products “far more toxic” than glyphosate on its own
regulatory agencies around the world rely heavily on industry-sponsored research
targets a biological pathway found in plants but not in humans
The same pathway exists in many bacteria and fungi, including microorganisms that make up the human gut microbiome
glyphosate and glyphosate herbicides are definitely carcinogenic
We cannot set an acceptable daily safe intake limit

prohibitedInterpretations: The article says pure glyphosate is harmless or non-toxic.
Greater toxicity of commercial formulations is treated as inconsistent with alleged toxicity of glyphosate itself.
Regulatory and industry safety positions are presented as the article author's conclusion.
Antoniou's allegations and interpretations are converted into unattributed scientific consensus.
Animal findings are silently rewritten as demonstrated human clinical outcomes.
Temporal association, toxicity, and carcinogenicity are collapsed into interchangeable claims.
reviewNotes: Preserve nested attribution: Jill Erzen reports an interview in which Michael Antoniou describes studies, industry positions, and regulatory practices.
The pure-compound versus commercial-formulation distinction is an intentional qualification, not an internal contradiction.
